169.title: Noach: the cloak carried backward (Genesis 9:20–27)
169.hook: Noah drinks and falls; two sons cover him, walking backward
169.howItsDone: Jewish teachers read this passage alongside the Talmud's teaching that publicly shaming someone is like shedding blood, and use it to teach protecting others' dignity.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the covenant after the flood, and seven laws for the children of Noah. Your line was laws for everyone.

Everyone has seen someone at their worst. A relative at a wedding who had too much. A coworker who cried in the bathroom. A friend whose embarrassing video went around the group chat. In that moment you have a choice, and it happens fast. You can look. You can take a picture. You can tell everyone. Or you can quietly help cover it up and walk away. The Torah has a story about exactly that moment, and it happens to Noah, the whole-hearted man who just saved the world.
screen: `SOMEONE AT THEIR WORST.` → `LOOK, SHARE, OR COVER?` → `IT HAPPENS TO NOAH.`

segments.voice: After the flood, Noah becomes a farmer and plants a vineyard, the first vineyard in the Torah. He drinks the wine, gets drunk, and lies uncovered in his tent. The hero of the flood, lying exposed, and the Torah doesn't hide it. One of his sons, Ham, sees his father like that, and goes out and tells his two brothers. That's his whole act: he saw, and he told. Then Shem and Japheth take a garment, lay it on both their shoulders, and walk in backward. The text slows down: they "went backward, and covered the nakedness of their father," their faces turned away, so they never saw. It's an almost awkward picture: two grown men shuffling backward into a tent, holding a cloak between them, so they can help without looking. Rashi notices a small thing in the Hebrew. The verb for took is singular: he took. That teaches, Rashi says, that Shem moved first, with extra eagerness, and Japheth joined him. When Noah wakes, he blesses Shem and Japheth, and curses Canaan, Ham's son. That curse has a painful later history. Centuries after, some people twisted it, calling it the curse of Ham, to justify slavery. But the text curses Canaan, not Ham, and says nothing at all about skin or color. That reading was a misuse, and it did real harm. The story's own lesson is simpler. The rabbis taught that shaming someone in public is like shedding their blood. Noah's sons show the other way. When someone falls, you can bring a cloak, and turn your face.
screen: `NOAH PLANTS THE FIRST VINEYARD.` · `HAM SAW, AND TOLD.` · `TWO SONS WALK IN BACKWARD.` · `A CURSE, LATER TWISTED.` · then, large: `WALK BACKWARD WITH THE CLOAK.`

segments.voice: Remember a time you saw someone embarrassed, or at their worst, and how you responded; then a time someone saw you like that, and covered for you, or didn't, and what that felt like. Now picture yourself walking backward into that moment, holding a cloak, face turned away, giving someone back their dignity.
Noach. The portion of Noah, where two sons walk backward with a cloak to cover their father without looking.
Your line: walk backward with the cloak. Dignity, carried on two pairs of shoulders. Until tomorrow.

170.title: Noach: ten generations of waiting (Avot 5:2)
170.hook: from Noah to Abraham ten generations pass with no one turning
170.tomorrow: Lech Lecha: the road ran everywhere
170.howItsDone: Pirkei Avot, the Ethics of the Fathers, is often studied on Shabbat afternoons; its fifth chapter's teachings on the ten generations are read alongside the genealogies at the end of the portion of Noach.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two sons walking backward with a cloak, covering their father without looking. Your line was walk backward with the cloak. Today, the portion of Noah ends.

Some changes move slower than a lifetime. A habit that won't break. A family pattern that shows up in the grandparents, then the parents, then the kids. A cause that moves an inch a decade. After long enough, it starts to sound like this: if it hasn't changed by now, it never will. The end of the portion of Noah is mostly lists of names: nations, cities, a tower that never gets finished, then more names. It's easy to skim. But a teaching in Pirkei Avot counts those names, and finds something in them about waiting.
screen: `SLOWER THAN A LIFETIME.` → `LISTS OF NAMES, EASY TO SKIM.` → `PIRKEI AVOT COUNTS THEM.`

segments.voice: Pirkei Avot says: there were ten generations from Adam to Noah, to show how patient God is. All those generations kept provoking God, until God brought the flood. Then ten generations from Noah to Abraham, to show how patient God is. All those generations kept provoking God, until Abraham came and received the reward of them all. Ten generations, twice over. A long wait for one person to turn. And the two lists end differently: the first in a flood, the second in Abraham. Same patience, different ending. What changed? Someone finally turned. The portion itself shows the waiting. After the flood, people build a city and a tower to reach the heavens, to make a name for themselves, and God scatters them. Then come the names again. And at the very end, a small detail. Abraham's father, Terah, takes his family and sets out from Ur toward the land of Canaan. They get as far as Haran, and stop, and settle there. Terah dies in Haran. He was headed in the right direction, and didn't arrive. The next portion begins with his son picking up the road. So this portion ends in the middle of a journey. That's what a slow change looks like here: generation after generation, and nothing. A father who starts and stops. Then a son who keeps going.
screen: `TEN GENERATIONS FROM ADAM TO NOAH.` · `TEN MORE, UNTIL ABRAHAM CAME.` · `A TOWER, AND MORE NAMES.` · `TERAH SETS OUT, AND STOPS IN HARAN.` · then, large: `TEN GENERATIONS.`

segments.voice: Think of one change you've been waiting for, in yourself or in someone you love, and notice the impatience: the sigh, the it'll never happen. Let it be there, then remember Terah stopping in Haran, and his son picking up the road. Maybe you're the one who starts, maybe the one who keeps going; either way, the road isn't wasted.
Noach. The portion of Noah: a whole-hearted man, a window, laws for everyone, a cloak, and ten generations of waiting.
Your line: ten generations. And with that, the portion of Noah is done. Tomorrow, the road picks up again.

171.title: Lech Lecha: the road ran everywhere
171.hook: a man leaves home, and his family's road runs to Kochi, Mumbai and the mountains of Ethiopia
171.howItsDone: Jewish communities around the world, Ashkenazi, Sephardi, Mizrahi, Indian, Ethiopian and many more, read the same weekly Torah portion, each with its own melodies, foods, customs and languages.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ten generations of waiting, and Terah stopping in Haran. Your line was ten generations. Now his son picks up the road: Lech Lecha.

Three scenes. In Kochi, on the southwest coast of India, a synagogue more than four hundred years old has a floor of hand-painted blue and white tiles from China. Up the coast near Mumbai, a community of oil pressers was known for generations by a nickname: the Saturday oil-men, because they would not work on Saturday. And in the mountains of Ethiopia, once a year, people climb to a high place in white clothes to pray and renew a promise. Every one of these is a Jewish scene. Today's portion opens with the man whose leaving started it all.
screen: `TILES FROM CHINA, IN KOCHI.` → `THE SATURDAY OIL-MEN.` → `A MOUNTAIN IN ETHIOPIA.`

segments.voice: You met the call itself on day thirty-seven: "Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house." And then, simply: "So Abram went." The family story of the Jewish people begins with someone leaving home, and the road didn't stop with him. Over the centuries Jewish families settled almost everywhere, and each community kept the same Torah while cooking, singing and dressing like its neighbors. You may know the Ashkenazi branch best: central and eastern Europe, Yiddish, the words you met on day three. Sephardi Jews trace their families to Spain and Portugal, and after 1492 carried their Judeo-Spanish language across the Mediterranean. Mizrahi Jews lived for many centuries in Iraq, Iran, Yemen, Syria and North Africa; the Jews of Iraq trace their community back to the exile in Babylon. In India there are several communities. The Jews of Cochin, with that tiled synagogue. The Bene Israel near Mumbai, whose tradition says their ancestors were shipwrecked on the coast long ago, and who kept Shabbat when they had almost nothing else. And Baghdadi Jews, traders who came later to Mumbai and Kolkata. In Ethiopia, the Beta Israel kept the Torah in the old Ge'ez language, led by their own priests, and fifty days after Yom Kippur they climb a mountain for the festival of Sigd. Today many of these families live in Israel, North America and around the world. So if Jewish brings to mind bagels and Yiddish, that's real, and it's one branch of a very big tree.
screen: `SO ABRAM WENT.` · `ASHKENAZI, SEPHARDI, MIZRAHI.` · `COCHIN, BENE ISRAEL, BAGHDADI.` · `BETA ISRAEL AND SIGD.`

segments.voice: Picture a map of the world, starting where Abram started, between two rivers. Let little lights come on: Kochi, Mumbai, Baghdad, Sana'a, Fez, Seville, Vilna, a mountain in Ethiopia, a street near you, each a kitchen, a synagogue, a family keeping Shabbat its own way. Stay with whichever one surprises you; if you pray, pray for every one of those tables.
Lech Lecha. Go forth: the call to Abram, and the start of a road that led Jewish families to nearly every corner of the world.
Your line: the road ran everywhere. One man left home, and his family's story now speaks many languages. Day one hundred seventy-one.

172.title: Lech Lecha: be a blessing (Genesis 12:2)
172.hook: Abram is told not only to be blessed but "be thou a blessing"
172.howItsDone: Jewish teachers often read 'be thou a blessing' as a charge to every Jew to bring good into the world, and the verse is frequently quoted in sermons on this portion and at life-cycle events.

segments.voice: Yesterday, lech lecha: one man left home, and the road ran to Kochi, Mumbai and the mountains of Ethiopia. Your line was the road ran everywhere.

People say it all the time now, sometimes with a hashtag: so blessed. A new job, a vacation photo, a good cup of coffee. Hashtag blessed. It means: good things came to me. And that's real; gratitude is good. But notice where the blessing stops. It lands on you, and there it stays. Right after God tells Abram to go, God makes him a string of promises: a great nation, blessing, a great name. And then, at the end, a short phrase that turns the whole thing around and sends the blessing out the door.
screen: `HASHTAG BLESSED.` → `IT LANDS ON YOU, AND STAYS.` → `A PHRASE THAT TURNS IT AROUND.`

segments.voice: The verse: "And I will make of thee a great nation, and I will bless thee, and make thy name great; and be thou a blessing." In Hebrew, veheyeh bracha, and grammatically it's an imperative. Not a prediction, not you'll turn out to be a blessing. A command: be one. Abram isn't only a place where blessing arrives. He's meant to be a place where it flows out. The next verse makes it wider: "and in thee shall all the families of the earth be blessed." All the families, not only his own. Rashi, drawing on the midrash, reads a handover here. Until now, blessings were in God's hands: God blessed Adam, God blessed Noah. From now on, God tells Abram, the blessings are given into your hands; you bless whomever you want. In this reading, a human being is trusted with blessing. And the word bracha may already be familiar. It's the name for what Jews say over bread, over wine, over a new season, and every one of those blessings is said by a person. In Rashi's reading, that human work of blessing starts here, with Abram. The portion shows what it looks like. In a few chapters Abram will throw open his tent to three strangers and run to feed them. He'll argue with God to save a city that isn't his. Being blessed is something that happens to you. Being a blessing is something you do.

173.title: Lech Lecha: not a thread (Genesis 14:22–23)
173.hook: Abram refuses the spoils of Sodom, not even a thread or a shoe-latchet
173.howItsDone: Jewish ethical teaching points to Abram's refusal of Sodom's spoils as a model of integrity, and the Talmud links it to the mitzvot of tzitzit and tefillin.

segments.voice: Yesterday, veheyeh bracha: not only blessed, but be a blessing. Your line was be a blessing.

Someone offers you something you didn't quite earn. A gift from a person who'll want a favor later. Credit for a project someone else mostly did. A discount you know is a mistake. It's right there, taking it would be easy, and nobody would really blame anyone for it. In the middle of Lech Lecha, Abram is offered a whole city's wealth. He did win it, in battle. The king himself tells him to keep it. Here's what he says instead.
screen: `SOMETHING YOU DIDN'T QUITE EARN.` → `A WHOLE CITY'S WEALTH.` → `WHAT ABRAM SAYS INSTEAD.`

segments.voice: Four kings make war on five kings, including the king of Sodom. Sodom loses. The victors carry off its people and its goods, and among the captives is Abram's nephew Lot. Abram hears, gathers three hundred eighteen men from his household, chases the kings as far as Dan, attacks by night, and brings everything back: Lot, the people, the goods. Now Abram is the hero, holding all of Sodom's wealth. The king of Sodom comes out to meet him with an offer that sounds generous: give me the people, and keep the goods for yourself. Abram answers that he has lifted up his hand to God, Maker of heaven and earth, "that I will not take a thread nor a shoe-latchet nor aught that is thine, lest thou shouldest say: I have made Abram rich." Not even a sandal strap. Why so absolute? He says it himself: so no one can say Sodom made him rich. Sodom, a city the Torah has already called wicked. Abram doesn't want his fortune tied to that name. His blessing comes from God, or not at all. And he isn't stingy with others. He sets aside what his young men have eaten, and says his allies, Aner, Eshcol and Mamre, should take their portion. His own principle doesn't cost anyone else. The Talmud adds a lovely twist. Because Abram refused a thread and a strap, it says, his descendants were given a thread and a strap: the blue thread of the tzitzit, the fringes, and the strap of the tefillin, from earlier on this path. The thread he wouldn't take from Sodom comes back to his children as a mitzvah.

segments.voice: Look honestly at this week: is there anything, even something tiny, that you took or kept but didn't really earn? Credit, a perk, a borrowed thing never returned, a benefit from someone you don't respect. Don't beat yourself up; just notice it, then imagine setting it down, and how light your hands feel.

174.title: Lech Lecha: between the pieces (Genesis 15)
174.hook: a vision in deep darkness, a smoking furnace, and a promise of exile and return
174.howItsDone: Jews call Genesis 15 the brit bein habetarim, the covenant between the pieces, and recall it at the Passover seder in the Haggadah's passage on God keeping the promise to Abraham.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abram refused Sodom's wealth: not a thread, not a sandal strap. Your line was not even a thread.

Some promises are quick: I'll call you back in five minutes. Some take years. A parent who plants a tree knowing they'll never sit in its shade. Someone saving for a grandchild who isn't born yet. There's a strange feeling in those promises: you believe them, and you know you won't see them come true. Abram has been promised a land and a great nation. Years have passed. He's still childless. One night God speaks to him again, and the promise gets much longer, and much darker, before it gets bright. It's called the covenant between the pieces.
screen: `A TREE YOU'LL NEVER SIT UNDER.` → `YEARS PASS. STILL NO CHILD.` → `THE PROMISE GETS LONGER.`

segments.voice: It begins with God saying: fear not, Abram, I am thy shield. And Abram answers honestly: what good is any of it? I have no child. So God brings him outside, under the night sky: "Look now toward heaven, and count the stars, if thou be able to count them." So shall your descendants be. The Torah says Abram believed, and God counted it to him as righteousness. Then comes something ancient and strange. God tells Abram to bring a heifer, a goat, a ram, a turtledove and a young pigeon. Abram cuts the animals in half and lays the halves opposite each other, with a path between. Birds of prey swoop down on the carcasses, and Abram drives them away. In the ancient Near East, this is how you sealed a covenant: the parties walked between the pieces, as if to say, may this happen to me if I break my word. The sun goes down. A deep sleep falls on Abram, and a great dark dread. In the darkness, God tells him the hard part. Your descendants will be strangers in a land not theirs, enslaved and afflicted four hundred years. Then that nation will be judged, and they'll come out with great wealth, and return here. Then, in the dark, a smoking furnace and a flaming torch pass between the pieces. Only God passes through. Abram doesn't. The promise is one-sided. At the Passover seder, Jews still read about this night: God kept the promise made to Abraham between the pieces. The promise was long. It went through darkness. And it came true.

175.title: Lech Lecha: new names (Genesis 17)
175.hook: Abram becomes Abraham, Sarai becomes Sarah, and the covenant of circumcision begins
175.howItsDone: Jewish boys are named at their brit milah on the eighth day, and girls are often named in the synagogue at a Torah reading or at a naming ceremony; Jews are called to the Torah by their Hebrew names.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the covenant between the pieces: count the stars, and a torch in the dark. Your line was the promise is long. Today, the last day of Lech Lecha.

A person can collect a lot of names in one life. The one on the birth certificate. A childhood nickname. The name a grandmother used. A name taken later, at a wedding, at a conversion, or just in growing up. Names aren't only labels. They carry who someone was, and sometimes who they're becoming. Abram is ninety-nine years old. He's been Abram his whole life. And God tells him that name is too small now. And the name grows by a single letter.
screen: `A LOT OF NAMES IN ONE LIFE.` → `WHO YOU WERE, WHO YOU'RE BECOMING.` → `A NAME GROWS BY ONE LETTER.`

segments.voice: God appears to Abram and says: walk before me, and be whole-hearted. Then: "Neither shall thy name any more be called Abram, but thy name shall be Abraham; for the father of a multitude of nations have I made thee." The verse itself explains the new name: Abraham, av hamon goyim, father of a multitude of nations. The change is one Hebrew letter: a heh, added in the middle. Then Sarai. God says: don't call her Sarai any more; Sarah shall be her name. She'll be blessed, and have a son, and be a mother of nations and kings. The Talmud reads Sarai as my princess, and Sarah as princess: at first she was a princess only to her own people; now she's a princess for the whole world. The ending that meant mine is dropped. She stops belonging to one household and starts belonging to everyone. Her name also changes by one letter: the yod at the end becomes a heh. Some teachers notice that heh is also a letter in God's name, and read it as if God gave each of them a piece of it. The Talmud goes further: Bar Kappara says that whoever still calls Abraham Abram transgresses a commandment. The new name is meant to stick. The same chapter begins the covenant of circumcision, brit milah, for Abraham and his household, and for every Jewish boy on the eighth day. By custom, that's when a Jewish boy is named: a covenant and a name, given together. So that's Lech Lecha, finished. The road ran everywhere. Be a blessing. Not a thread. A long promise in the dark. And a name that grows.
screen: `ABRAM BECOMES ABRAHAM.` · `SARAI BECOMES SARAH.` · `A HEH FOR EACH OF THEM.` · `A COVENANT AND A NAME TOGETHER.` · then, large: `A NAME CAN GROW.`

segments.voice: Say your name silently, slowly, the way someone who loves you would say it, and notice what it carries: who named you, what it means, the people who've said it kindly. Then ask who you're growing into, and imagine a letter added to your name, a small piece of something larger. Say your name once more, with that in it.
